newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Iberia shuts door on shaky past with ties.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Iberia shuts door on shaky past with ties.

text.p: Spain announced on Friday that flagship airline Iberia has signed key alliances in Europe and North America, seeking to close the door on its troubled past and set the stage for its privatisation.

Iberia, on the verge of collapse just two years ago amid high costs and souring Latin American investments, signed long-promised preliminary agreements with British Airways and U.S.-based American Airlines.
Both carriers have an option to buy a minority stake in Iberia by December 31, kicking off the state-owned group's privatisation, state holding group SEPI said.

"(This will) strengthen (Iberia's) market position at home, assuring and extending its leadership in traffic between Europe and Latin America, as well as increasing its presence in the European, North Atlantic and Asian markets," SEPI said.
Both commercial deals foresee the establishment of agreements on code-sharing, frequent-flyer programmes, cargo operations and other areas where services can be improved.
"The agreements, once developed, will permit Iberia to increase its offer of flights and international connections... in what will be one of the world's biggest networks of global routes," SEPI said.

Iberia, which has faced a rocky road to renewed profitability, turned a profit of 3.5 billion pesetas ($23.2 million) in 1996 after narrowing its loss by 75 percent in 1995 from 41.5 billion a year earlier.
"It (the agreements) can only be good news. It might be a stimulus to move the Iberia project forward," an analyst in Madrid said.

At the end of June, Iberia chairman Xavier de Irala said Iberia was speaking with BA, Air France, KLM, Swissair and Alitalia on a European alliance, but apparently opted for the group that had been most exposed to fierce international competition.
For its U.S. alliance, Iberia was also considering a deal with Continental Airlines, SEPI said this spring.
"BA is twice the size of Iberia in terms of passenger carriers...American overall is the second largest in the world," said Kevin Fogarty, transport analyst at Daiwa Europe in London.
"What (Iberia) has to gain is a truly global partnership."

In December 1995, the European Commission approved an emergency state cash injection of 87 billion pesetas to save Iberia from bankruptcy, but required the group to rid itself of the bulk of its Latin American holdings.

Iberia had to cut most of its 85 percent stake in Aerolineas Argentinas, whose losses had dragged Iberia deep into the red, along with its shares in Argentine domestic airline Austral and Chile's Ladeco. Iberia also had a holding in Venezuela's Viasa.
Chilean airline Ladeco said in April that Iberia would sell its 38 percent stake in the carrier, and shareholders in Venezuela's Viasa agreed to liquidate this loss-making airline within a year.

In Friday's announcement, SEPI also said American would buy 10 percent of Aerolineas Argentinas and its local sister Austral, while Iberia would keep 10 percent in the group. ($ = 151.0 Spanish Pesetas)
